chapters.title: Justice in the Ruins
beats: In the wake of global devastation and tens of millions dead, the victorious Allied powers gathered in Germany to place the surviving leaders of the defeated regime on trial.
The tribunal sought to establish international law by prosecuting state leaders for aggressive war and atrocities against civilian populations.
Yet just hours before the sentences of death were to be carried out by hanging, the highest-ranking defendant delivered a final, calculated shock to the court.

chapters.title: The Rise and the Reckoning
beats: In Munich during the early 1920s, Hermann Göring joined the Nazi Party and aligned himself with Adolf Hitler, seeking to build an authoritarian German state.
Hitler named Göring to key ministerial posts in Berlin and formally declared that if anything should befall him, Göring was his designated successor.
Nuremberg was chosen by the Allies as the seat of the international military tribunal to hold these leaders accountable before the world.
Robert H. Jackson, leading the prosecution for the United States, came to Nuremberg determined to secure convictions for crimes against humanity.

chapters.title: From Total Power to Total Defeat
beats: Göring marched with Hitler in Munich in November 1923 during the Beer Hall Putsch, where Göring was shot and wounded before the party's eventual rise to power.
After Hitler took power in Berlin in 1933, Göring was appointed Minister-President of Prussia and established sweeping control over German economic and military mobilization.

During the war, Göring commanded the air force and promised hundreds of tons of daily supplies to surrounded German forces at Stalingrad, but deliveries fell drastically short and thousands surrendered.
By April 1945, as defeat closed in, Hitler admitted the war was lost, while Göring was ordered arrested after a leadership dispute before Germany formally surrendered in May.

chapters.title: The Clash in Courtroom 600
beats: The Nuremberg trials opened in November 1945, where Robert H. Jackson confronted Göring over state-sponsored deportation, enslavement, and mass extermination.
Göring mounted a combative defense from the prisoner dock, seeking to justify the regime's actions and challenge the jurisdiction of the Allied tribunal.
On October 1, 1946, the tribunal delivered its verdict, finding Göring guilty on all counts and sentencing him to die by hanging.

chapters.title: The Final Act
beats: Following his death sentence at Nuremberg, Göring petitioned the tribunal to be executed by a military firing squad rather than the gallows.
The Allied authorities denied the request, keeping Göring confined under round-the-clock guard in his prison cell as execution preparations proceeded.
On the night of October 15, 1946, mere hours before the hangings were scheduled to begin, Göring ingested a concealed cyanide capsule.
Guards discovered him dying in his cell, thwarting the court's plan to carry out the death sentence by hanging.

chapters.title: The Legacy of the Tribunal
beats: With the death of Hermann Göring, the Nuremberg proceedings against the principal leaders concluded in October 1946.
Jackson and the Allied representatives established the legal precedent that political and military commanders could be held personally accountable for state actions.
The proceedings formalized the legal standard of crimes against humanity agreed upon in 1945, cementing the framework of the Nuremberg Charter in international law.
